projects.overview: ONE MORE SPIN turns European roulette into a roguelike. Each round gives you a limited number of spins to reach a score quota; you place chips on numbers and outside bets, cash in on the result and spend coins in a shop on relics and chip upgrades that bend the odds. The jam themes were "Spin to Win" and "Very Serious". We built the jam version in six days as a team of two and are now developing it further.
built: GameManager singleton that owns the game state: rounds, spins, quota, coins and progression
Bet system based on a list of active bets, so any number of chips can be placed and resolved independently per spin
Drag-and-drop chip placement on the betting table, with correct layering while dragging
Animated feedback with Tweens: payout popups, a quota counter that counts up, overlays chained via callbacks
Between-round shop with relics and chip upgrades
Options menu with music/SFX sliders on separate audio buses, saved with ConfigFile and reachable from main menu and pause menu
projects.challenge: Our first version updated the UI the moment a spin was resolved, so numbers changed before the animations had played – the game felt out of sync and the round sometimes advanced too early. We separated game state from presentation: the state updates immediately, but the labels only change at the end of each Tween, and the next step (overlay, win sound, next round) is triggered by a callback when the animation is done. That made every spin read clearly and fixed the round-counting bugs along the way.
projects.differently: Roulette produces only one number per spin, so there are just a handful of things that can trigger. Games like Balatro feel exciting because rewards cascade one after another. For the post-jam version I'm designing modifiers that each trigger on their own, so late-game spins build up into a chain of escalating feedback instead of a single payout.

projects.title: Camping Diorama
projects.tagline: A stylized 3D scene made solo – from Blender modelling and wind rigs to Substance texturing and UE5 rendering.

facts.role: Solo – modelling, UV mapping, rigging, texturing, scene assembly, lighting & rendering

projects.overview: A complete stylized diorama built end to end on my own: every asset modelled in Blender, UV-unwrapped and textured in Substance Painter, rigged for wind animation and assembled, lit and rendered in Unreal Engine 5. The tent serves as the hero asset.
built: Modelled every asset in Blender, with the tent as the hero asset
UV mapping and a stylized low-poly texturing pipeline in Substance Painter
Bone-based wind rigs for deformation animation
Scripted FBX export from Blender to Unreal Engine
Master material setup, scene assembly and lighting in UE5
Animated camera showcase rendered with the Level Sequencer
projects.challenge: I started this project without real experience in any of the three tools. The biggest challenge was learning Blender, Substance Painter and Unreal Engine 5 well enough – in a short, fixed timeframe of around 75 hours – to use them properly instead of just getting something on screen. I solved it by focusing on a clean pipeline early: a consistent stylized texturing approach, a scripted FBX export and one master material in UE5, so each new asset went through the same steps instead of being solved from scratch.

projects.tagline: Two published client-side mods for challenge runs – Challenge Timer and All Items.

projects.overview: Two client-side Fabric mods for singleplayer challenge runs, the kind known from Let's Plays. Challenge Timer shows a run timer above the hotbar. All Items challenges you to collect every item in the game, one at a time, in random order. Both are published on Modrinth and support Minecraft 26.2 and 26.3.
built: Challenge Timer: real-time run timer that pauses in the pause menu, scales its format from seconds to days and is fully controlled by commands
All Items: the item pool is read from the game registry at runtime – nothing is hardcoded, so it always matches the installed version
Seed-based random order, automatic detection in inventory, off-hand and armour slots, and a warning for items that can't be obtained in survival
Scrollable overview grid that lists remaining items alphabetically, so the upcoming order stays hidden
Custom HUD rendering with configurable hex colour and background, plus progress saved per world
Ported both mods to a new Minecraft version and its API changes (26.2 → 26.3)
projects.challenge: The gameplay logic itself was straightforward. The trickier part was the step from a mod that runs in my own development environment to a public release that installs and works for everyone right away – packaging it correctly, declaring the right dependencies and versions, and publishing it on Modrinth so players can simply drop it into their mods folder.

projects.overview: Ashoka, partnering with the Campus Wellbeing Project, asked our course to develop a game that supports the project's message. Our answer is an endless runner in the style of Subway Surfers: you run across campus and have to keep collecting orbs for Energy, Social and Balance – if one of them runs empty, the run is over. The game runs in any browser and is now used at campuses worldwide. I was responsible for the programming in a team of five.
built: The complete game code in plain JavaScript – no engine, runs in any browser including phones
Three-lane runner movement and continuous forward scrolling
Energy, Social and Balance meters that drain over time and refill with collected orbs – the core lose condition
Obstacle and pickup spawning, distance tracking and the results screen
Integration of the team's art and UI into a mobile-friendly portrait layout
